Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.

- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. - Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

Invoke a skill.

- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

"""Compute drag coefficient, Reynolds, Froude, and Strouhal numbers per run.

Water properties are evaluated at the logged water temperature of each run.
Runs whose post-run zero differs from the pre-run tare by more than
DRIFT_LIMIT_N are flagged and excluded from the summary statistics.

Outputs results/cd.csv, results/summary.json, and LaTeX snippets in
paper/generated/ for the manuscript.
"""

import json
import os

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

OUT_DIR = "results"
TEX_DIR = "paper/generated"

G = 9.81
L = 0.60  # m, submerged length of cylinder
TANK_WIDTH = 0.90  # m
TANK_DEPTH = 0.75  # m
DRIFT_LIMIT_N = 0.05
MASKELL_EPS = 2.5  # Maskell (1963) blockage factor, for an indicative correction


def water_viscosity(T):
    """Dynamic viscosity (Pa s), Kestin et al. (1978) correlation."""
    dT = 20.0 - T
    log_ratio = dT / (T + 96) * (1.2378 - 1.303e-3 * dT + 3.06e-6 * dT**2
                                 + 2.55e-8 * dT**3)
    return 1.002e-3 * 10**log_ratio


def water_density(T):
    """Density (kg/m^3), Tanaka et al. (2001) formula for air-free water."""
    a1, a2, a3, a4, a5 = -3.983035, 301.797, 522528.9, 69.34881, 999.974950
    return a5 * (1 - (T + a1) ** 2 * (T + a2) / (a3 * (T + a4)))


forces = pd.read_csv(os.path.join(OUT_DIR, "forces.csv"))
log = pd.read_csv("data/run_log.csv").rename(columns={"run_id": "run"})
df = forces.merge(log, on="run", validate="one_to_one")

D = df.diameter_mm / 1000
U = df.speed_m_s
df["rho"] = water_density(df.water_temp_c)
df["nu"] = water_viscosity(df.water_temp_c) / df.rho
df["Re"] = U * D / df.nu
df["Fr_D"] = U / np.sqrt(G * D)
q_area = 0.5 * df.rho * U**2 * D * L
df["Cd"] = df.F_mean_N / q_area
df["Cd_sem"] = df.F_sem_N / q_area
df["Cd_rms"] = df.F_std_N / q_area
df["St"] = df.f_peak_Hz / 2 * D / U  # drag fluctuates at twice the shedding freq.
df["blockage"] = D * L / (TANK_WIDTH * TANK_DEPTH)
df["Cd_maskell"] = df.Cd / (1 + MASKELL_EPS * df.Cd * df.blockage)
df["excluded"] = df.zero_drift_N.abs() > DRIFT_LIMIT_N
df.to_csv(os.path.join(OUT_DIR, "cd.csv"), index=False)

good = df[~df.excluded]
cyl_order = ["1in", "1.5in", "2in"]
by_cyl = {}
for cyl in cyl_order:
    g = good[good.cylinder == cyl]
    by_cyl[cyl] = {
        "D_mm": float(g.diameter_mm.iloc[0]),
        "aspect_ratio": float(L / (g.diameter_mm.iloc[0] / 1000)),
        "blockage": float(g.blockage.iloc[0]),
        "n_runs": int(len(g)),
        "Cd_mean": float(g.Cd.mean()),
        "Cd_std": float(g.Cd.std()),
        "Cd_maskell_mean": float(g.Cd_maskell.mean()),
        "Re_min": float(g.Re.min()),
        "Re_max": float(g.Re.max()),
        "T_min": float(g.water_temp_c.min()),
        "T_max": float(g.water_temp_c.max()),
    }

# Re that would have been reported with the old fixed 20 C viscosity
re_20c_bias = float((U * D / 1.004e-6 / df.Re - 1).loc[~df.excluded].mean())
excluded = df[df.excluded]
with open(os.path.join(OUT_DIR, "calibration.json")) as f:
    cals = json.load(f)
rel_sens_err = {
    f: s["sensitivity_std_err"] / s["sensitivity_V_per_N"] for f, s in cals.items()
}
cd_vs_fr = np.polyfit(good.Fr_D, good.Cd, 1)
summary = {
    "n_runs": int(len(df)),
    "n_good": int(len(good)),
    "excluded_runs": excluded.run.tolist(),
    "excluded_drift_N": excluded.zero_drift_N.round(3).tolist(),
    "max_drift_good_N": float(good.zero_drift_N.abs().max()),
    "Cd_mean_all": float(good.Cd.mean()),
    "Cd_std_all": float(good.Cd.std()),
    "Cd_maskell_mean_all": float(good.Cd_maskell.mean()),
    "Cd_excluded_run": excluded.Cd.round(3).tolist(),
    "Cd_sem_max_rel": float((good.Cd_sem / good.Cd).max()),
    "Cd_rms_mean_rel": float((good.Cd_rms / good.Cd).mean()),
    "Re_min": float(good.Re.min()),
    "Re_max": float(good.Re.max()),
    "Fr_min": float(good.Fr_D.min()),
    "Fr_max": float(good.Fr_D.max()),
    "Cd_vs_Fr_slope": float(cd_vs_fr[0]),
    "Cd_vs_Fr_corr": float(np.corrcoef(good.Fr_D, good.Cd)[0, 1]),
    "Cd_vs_Re_corr": float(np.corrcoef(np.log(good.Re), good.Cd)[0, 1]),
    "St_mean": float(good.St.mean()),
    "St_std": float(good.St.std()),
    "re_20c_bias": re_20c_bias,
    "sensitivity_rel_err_max": float(max(rel_sens_err.values())),
    "by_cylinder": by_cyl,
}
with open(os.path.join(OUT_DIR, "summary.json"), "w") as f:
    json.dump(summary, f, indent=2)

# LaTeX macros so numbers in the text always match the pipeline output
os.makedirs(TEX_DIR, exist_ok=True)

    "NGood": f"{summary['n_good']}",
    "ExcludedRun": f"{summary['excluded_runs'][0]}" if len(excluded) else "none",

    "ReMin": f"{summary['Re_min'] / 1e3:.1f}",
    "ReMax": f"{summary['Re_max'] / 1e3:.1f}",
    "FrMin": f"{summary['Fr_min']:.2f}",
    "FrMax": f"{summary['Fr_max']:.2f}",

    "SensB": f"{cals['loadcell_2026-03.csv']['sensitivity_V_per_N']:.5f}",
    "CalResidMax": f"{max(c['max_resid_N'] for c in cals.values()) * 1000:.0f}",
    "CalMaxLoad": f"{max(c['max_load_N'] for c in cals.values()):.1f}",
    "FMaxGood": f"{good.F_mean_N.max():.1f}",
    "SubLength": f"{L:.2f}",

    "TankWidth": f"{TANK_WIDTH:.2f}",
    "TankDepth": f"{TANK_DEPTH:.2f}",
    "MaskellEps": f"{MASKELL_EPS:.1f}",

for cyl, s in by_cyl.items():
    n = names[cyl]
    macros[f"Cd{n}"] = f"{s['Cd_mean']:.3f}"

"""Reduce raw tow tank load cell time series to mean drag force per run.

Handles both DAQ file formats (comma-separated with a commented header for
the 2025 batches, semicolon-separated for the 2026 batch) and fits the load
cell sensitivity from the calibration file in effect on the run date.

Outputs results/forces.csv and results/calibration.json.
"""

import glob
import json
import os

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

RAW_DIR = "data/raw"
CAL_DIR = "data/calibration"
OUT_DIR = "results"

G = 9.81
FS = 200.0  # Hz, sample rate for both DAQ versions
TARE_WINDOW = (0.0, 1.0)  # s, carriage at rest before the run
STEADY_WINDOW = (3.0, 8.0)  # s, constant carriage speed
POST_WINDOW = (11.0, 12.0)  # s, carriage at rest after the run
N_BLOCKS = 5  # blocks for standard error of the steady-state mean

# Calibration in effect for each batch (load cell remounted 2026-03-10)
CALIBRATIONS = {
    "2025-10-14": "loadcell_2025-09.csv",
    "2025-11-03": "loadcell_2025-09.csv",
    "2026-03-12": "loadcell_2026-03.csv",
}


def fit_calibration(fname):
    cal = pd.read_csv(os.path.join(CAL_DIR, fname))
    force = cal.mass_g / 1000 * G
    (slope, intercept), cov = np.polyfit(force, cal.voltage_V, 1, cov=True)
    resid = cal.voltage_V - (slope * force + intercept)
    return {
        "file": fname,
        "sensitivity_V_per_N": float(slope),
        "sensitivity_std_err": float(np.sqrt(cov[0, 0])),
        "offset_V": float(intercept),
        "max_resid_N": float(np.abs(resid).max() / slope),
        "max_load_N": float(force.max()),
        "n_points": len(cal),
    }


def read_run(fname):
    """Return (time_s, voltage_V) for either DAQ file format."""
    with open(fname) as f:
        first = f.readline()
    if ";" in first:
        d = pd.read_csv(fname, sep=";")
        return d.t.values, d.V.values
    d = pd.read_csv(fname, comment="#")
    return d.time_s.values, d.loadcell_V.values


def in_window(t, window):
    return (t >= window[0]) & (t < window[1])


def dominant_frequency(x):
    n = np.arange(len(x))
    x = x - np.polyval(np.polyfit(n, x, 1), n)
    power = np.abs(np.fft.rfft(x * np.hanning(len(x)))) ** 2
    freqs = np.fft.rfftfreq(len(x), 1 / FS)
    return freqs[np.argmax(power[1:]) + 1]


cals = {name: fit_calibration(name) for name in sorted(set(CALIBRATIONS.values()))}
for c in cals.values():
    print(f"{c['file']}: sensitivity = {c['sensitivity_V_per_N']:.5f} V/N")

rows = []
for batch, cal_file in CALIBRATIONS.items():
    sens = cals[cal_file]["sensitivity_V_per_N"]
    for fname in sorted(glob.glob(os.path.join(RAW_DIR, batch, "run_*.csv"))):
        t, v = read_run(fname)
        tare = v[in_window(t, TARE_WINDOW)].mean()
        post = v[in_window(t, POST_WINDOW)].mean()
        force = (v - tare) / sens
        steady = force[in_window(t, STEADY_WINDOW)]
        block_means = np.array([b.mean() for b in np.array_split(steady, N_BLOCKS)])
        rows.append({
            "run": int(os.path.basename(fname)[4:7]),
            "batch": batch,
            "calibration": cal_file,
            "sensitivity_V_per_N": sens,
            "F_mean_N": steady.mean(),
            "F_std_N": steady.std(),
            "F_sem_N": block_means.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(N_BLOCKS),
            "zero_drift_N": (post - tare) / sens,
            "f_peak_Hz": dominant_frequency(steady),
        })

os.makedirs(OUT_DIR, exist_ok=True)
out = pd.DataFrame(rows).sort_values("run")
out.to_csv(os.path.join(OUT_DIR, "forces.csv"), index=False)
with open(os.path.join(OUT_DIR, "calibration.json"), "w") as f:
    json.dump(cals, f, indent=2)
print(f"Processed {len(out)} runs")

% Numbers below are generated by scripts/analyze.py from the raw data

\newcommand{\Fr}{\mathit{Fr}_D}

\title{Drag and vortex shedding of surface-piercing circular cylinders in a
towing tank}
\author{Pete Bachant\thanks{\todo{affiliation, co-authors (e.g., J.\ Rivera,
who wrote the original processing code, and whoever ran the 2025 campaigns)}}}
\date{\todo{date} \quad --- \quad first draft}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
We report mean drag and vortex-shedding frequency measurements on three
smooth circular cylinders (diameters 25.4, 38.1 and 50.8~mm) towed vertically
through a small towing tank with a fixed immersed length of \SubLength~m.
Thirty runs at carriage speeds of 0.2--1.1~m/s span Reynolds numbers of
$\Rey = \ReMin \times 10^3$--$\ReMax \times 10^3$ and diameter Froude
numbers of $\Fr = \FrMin$--$\FrMax$. Drag was measured with a single load
cell calibrated by dead weights before each campaign, and fluid properties
were evaluated at the measured water temperature of each run. One run was
rejected because its load cell zero drifted by \ExcludedDrift~N during the
run. The remaining \NGood{} runs give a mean drag coefficient of
$C_D = \CdMean \pm \CdStd$ (mean $\pm$ run-to-run standard deviation), with
no significant dependence on diameter. The in-line force oscillates at twice
the shedding frequency, giving a Strouhal number of $\St = \StMean \pm
\StStd$. The measured $C_D$ is at the upper end of the range reported for
two-dimensional cylinders in the subcritical regime; we discuss the
competing effects of tank blockage (\BlockageOne--\BlockageTwo\%), the free
end, and the free surface. \todo{one-sentence take-home once the framing is
settled}
\end{abstract}

%--Paper--

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

The flow past a circular cylinder is the canonical bluff-body problem, and
its mean drag coefficient in the subcritical regime ($10^3 \lesssim \Rey
\lesssim 2 \times 10^5$) is well established, at roughly
$C_D \approx 1.0$--$1.2$ for a nominally two-dimensional cylinder
\citep{Wieselsberger1921, Roshko1961, Zdravkovich1997}. Over the same range
the wake sheds vortices at a nearly constant Strouhal number
$\St \approx 0.2$ \citep{Williamson1996, Norberg2003}.

Towing-tank measurements depart from this ideal in several ways. The
cylinder pierces the free surface, so the free surface can deform and add
wave-making drag as the Froude number increases
\citep{ChaplinTeigen2003}. The submerged end is free, and the finite aspect
ratio changes the wake and lowers the sectional drag near the tip
\citep{FoxWest1993}. The model also occupies a finite fraction of the tank
cross-section, which accelerates the flow around it and raises the apparent
drag \citep{Maskell1963, WestApelt1982}.

\todo{State the motivation: e.g., commissioning/validating the facility,
providing a benchmark dataset, or a teaching laboratory. The framing decides
which of the discussion points below to emphasize.}
Here we report drag and shedding-frequency measurements on three cylinder
diameters at a fixed immersed length. Varying the diameter changes the
Reynolds number, Froude number, aspect ratio and blockage together, and we
use this to bound how large each effect can be.

\section{Experimental setup}
\label{sec:setup}

\subsection{Facility and models}

The experiments were carried out in a towing tank \TankWidth~m wide with a
water depth of \TankDepth~m. \todo{tank length, carriage drive and speed
control, how speed was verified, settling time between runs}. Three smooth
circular cylinders with nominal diameters of 1, 1.5 and 2~in (25.4, 38.1
and 50.8~mm) were mounted vertically on the carriage. Each pierced the free
surface and was immersed to a depth of $L = \SubLength$~m, leaving a gap of
\EndGap~m between the free end and the tank floor.
\todo{cylinder material, surface finish/roughness, end condition (flat?),
mounting and stiffness/natural frequency.} Table~\ref{tab:cylinders} gives
the parameters for each cylinder.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Test matrix and mean drag coefficient for each cylinder. $L/D$ is
the immersed aspect ratio and $B = DL/(WH)$ the frontal-area blockage ratio
for a tank of width $W$ and depth $H$. $C_D$ is given as mean $\pm$
run-to-run standard deviation; $C_{D,c}$ is the indicative
blockage-corrected value from \eqref{eq:maskell}.}
\label{tab:cylinders}
\small
\begin{tabular}{rcrrcccll}
\toprule
$D$ (mm) & Date & $L/D$ & $B$ (\%) & $T$ ($^\circ$C) & $\Rey/10^3$ &
Runs & $C_D$ & $C_{D,c}$ \\
\midrule

\end{tabular}

Each cylinder was towed at ten speeds from 0.2 to 1.1~m/s in steps of
0.1~m/s, one run per speed. The three campaigns took place on different
days (Table~\ref{tab:cylinders}). Water temperature, measured for each run
\todo{how and where measured}, ranged from 13.7 to 17.6~$^\circ$C across
the campaigns.

\subsection{Force measurement}

The in-line force was measured with a single-axis load cell
\todo{make, model, rated capacity, mounting arrangement} and recorded at
200~Hz for 12~s per run. The load cell was calibrated in situ by hanging
dead weights of 0--2~kg (0--\CalMaxLoad~N) in a loading and unloading
sequence. A linear fit gives sensitivities of \SensA~V/N for the
September~2025 calibration, used for the 25.4 and 50.8~mm cylinders, and
\SensB~V/N for the March~2026 calibration. The second calibration was made
after the load cell was remounted, and covers the 38.1~mm cylinder. In both
calibrations the largest residual about the linear fit is \CalResidMax~mN,
including any hysteresis between loading and unloading.

The largest mean drag measured (\FMaxGood~N, 50.8~mm cylinder at 1.1~m/s)
slightly exceeds the largest calibration load, so that point relies on a
short extrapolation of the linear fit. \todo{confirm linearity beyond
\CalMaxLoad~N from the load cell specification, or extend the calibration.}

\section{Data reduction}
\label{sec:reduction}

Figure~\ref{fig:timeseries} shows a typical force record. For each run the
load cell voltage averaged over the first second, with the carriage at rest,
is taken as the zero and subtracted. The mean drag $F_D$ is the average over
$3 \le t < 8$~s, where the carriage is moving at constant speed and the
start-up transient has passed. The drag coefficient, Reynolds number and
diameter Froude number are
\begin{equation}
C_D = \frac{F_D}{\tfrac{1}{2}\rho U^2 D L}, \qquad
\Rey = \frac{U D}{\nu}, \qquad
\Fr = \frac{U}{\sqrt{g D}},
\end{equation}
where $U$ is the carriage speed. The density $\rho$ and kinematic viscosity
$\nu$ are evaluated at each run's water temperature using the formulations
of \citet{Tanaka2001} and \citet{Kestin1978}. With $\nu$ fixed at its
20~$^\circ$C value instead, $\Rey$ would be overestimated by
\ReBiasPct\% on average, because the water was 2.4--6.3~$^\circ$C colder.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics{timeseries.pdf}
\caption{Drag force record for the 25.4~mm cylinder at $U = 0.6$~m/s.
The shaded band is the averaging window and the dashed line the mean
drag. The oscillation at constant speed is the in-line force at twice the
shedding frequency.}
\label{fig:timeseries}
\end{figure}

The shedding frequency $f_s$ is obtained from the force spectrum over the
same window. The in-line (drag) force fluctuates at $2 f_s$, so the
Strouhal number is $\St = f_{\mathrm{peak}} D / (2U)$, where
$f_{\mathrm{peak}}$ is the dominant spectral peak. A 5~s window gives a
frequency resolution of 0.2~Hz. This corresponds to an uncertainty in
$\St$ of up to about $\pm 0.01$ at the lowest speeds, and less at higher
speeds.

\paragraph{Run screening.}
The force after the carriage has stopped ($11 \le t < 12$~s) is compared
with the zero measured before the run. For \NGood{} of the \NRuns{} runs
the two agree within \MaxDriftGood~mN. In run~\ExcludedRun{}
(50.8~mm, 0.8~m/s) the reading drifts steadily through the run and ends
\ExcludedDrift~N above zero. This run was also flagged in the laboratory
log. Its apparent drag coefficient of \ExcludedCd{} is an outlier, and runs
with a zero shift above \DriftLimit~N are excluded from all averages.
\todo{repeat run 17 if the setup is still available.}

\subsection{Uncertainty}

Three components of the uncertainty in $C_D$ can be estimated from the
data:
\begin{itemize}
\item \emph{Random error of the mean within a run.} Block averaging over
five 1~s blocks gives a standard error of at most \CdSemMaxPct\% of $C_D$.
\item \emph{Calibration.} The standard error of the fitted sensitivity is
at most \SensErrPct\%.
\item \emph{Run-to-run repeatability.} The standard deviation of $C_D$
about the mean for each cylinder is 2--3\% (Table~\ref{tab:cylinders}).
\end{itemize}
The run-to-run scatter is about ten times larger than the within-run
random error. It must therefore come from run-to-run differences in the
conditions, such as residual tank motion from previous runs (noted in the
log for run~4) or small variations in carriage speed. We take it as the
measure of precision. \todo{add bias contributions from carriage speed
($C_D \propto U^{-2}$), immersed length and diameter tolerance, and combine
them following standard practice (e.g., GUM).}

\section{Results}
\label{sec:results}

\subsection{Drag coefficient}

Figure~\ref{fig:cd} shows the drag coefficients of all runs against
Reynolds and Froude numbers. Averaged over all \NGood{} accepted runs,
$C_D = \CdMean \pm \CdStd$. The means for the three cylinders
(\CdOne, \CdOneHalf{} and \CdTwo) differ by much less than the
run-to-run scatter. The aspect ratio varies by a factor of two and the
blockage ratio by a factor of two between cylinders, so within the
precision of these data, $C_D$ does not depend on diameter.

There is a weak upward trend of $C_D$ with speed. Over all accepted runs
the correlation coefficient of $C_D$ with $\ln \Rey$ is \CdReCorr, and with
$\Fr$ it is \CdFrCorr. The trend is clearest for the 25.4~mm cylinder,
which reaches the highest Froude numbers. For a single cylinder $\Rey$ and
$\Fr$ are both proportional to $U$, so the two cannot be separated within
one cylinder. Between cylinders, the 50.8~mm cylinder covers the largest
range of $\Rey$ at the smallest $\Fr$ and shows no clear trend.
\todo{decide whether the data support attributing the trend to $\Fr$; a
fit of $C_D$ against both parameters may help.}

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{cd.pdf}
\caption{Drag coefficient against (a) Reynolds number and (b) diameter
Froude number. The open symbol is run~\ExcludedRun, excluded because of
load cell zero drift.}
\label{fig:cd}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Strouhal number}

The force spectrum has a single dominant peak in every run, and the
corresponding Strouhal numbers are plotted in Fig.~\ref{fig:st}. Across
all cylinders and speeds $\St = \StMean \pm \StStd$, independent of
$\Rey$, $\Fr$ and diameter within the frequency resolution. This value
agrees with the established subcritical value of $\St \approx 0.2$
\citep{Williamson1996, Norberg2003}. It also indicates that the dominant
force fluctuation is vortex shedding rather than a structural or carriage
resonance.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics{strouhal.pdf}
\caption{Strouhal number from the dominant frequency of the in-line force,
$\St = f_{\mathrm{peak}} D/(2U)$. The dashed line is the mean over all
accepted runs.}
\label{fig:st}
\end{figure}

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Comparison with two-dimensional data.}
The measured $C_D = \CdMean$ is at the upper end of the
$C_D \approx 1.0$--$1.2$ range reported for nominally two-dimensional
cylinders at these Reynolds numbers \citep{Wieselsberger1921,
Zdravkovich1997}. Three effects specific to this setup push in different
directions.

\paragraph{Blockage.}
The frontal area of the immersed cylinder, $DL$, occupies
$B = \BlockageOne$--$\BlockageTwo$\% of the tank cross-section. As an
indication of the size of the effect, Maskell's correction
\citep{Maskell1963},
\begin{equation}
C_{D,c} = \frac{C_D}{1 + \varepsilon\, C_D\, B},
\label{eq:maskell}
\end{equation}
with $\varepsilon = \MaskellEps$, lowers the mean to
$C_{D,c} = \CdMaskellMean$. The corrected values for the three cylinders
(Table~\ref{tab:cylinders}) are more spread out than the uncorrected ones,
and the order is reversed, so that $C_{D,c}$ decreases with diameter.
Equation~\eqref{eq:maskell} was derived for closed wind tunnels. Its use
for a surface-piercing cylinder with a free end, in a tank with a free
surface, is uncertain. Some of the blocked fluid can escape through the
gap under the cylinder and by raising the free surface, so the
correction here is probably an upper bound. \todo{decide on a blockage
treatment, e.g.\ following \citet{WestApelt1982}, who found blockage
effects on circular cylinders to be small below $B \approx 6\%$; or report
uncorrected values only.}

\paragraph{Free end and aspect ratio.}
For cantilevered cylinders with a free end, the mean drag decreases as the
aspect ratio is reduced, because flow over the tip weakens the near-wake
suction \citep{FoxWest1993}. Here $L/D$ ranges from \AROne{} to \ARTwo{}.
A free-end effect alone would give the 50.8~mm cylinder the lowest $C_D$.
Instead the uncorrected means are flat in $D$, which is consistent with
the free-end and blockage effects partly cancelling.

\paragraph{Free surface.}
The diameter Froude number reaches \FrMax. At these Froude numbers the
free surface around a surface-piercing cylinder deforms strongly, with a
bow wave ahead and a depression behind, and the sectional drag near the
surface changes \citep{ChaplinTeigen2003}. The weak rise of $C_D$ with
speed, clearest for the smallest cylinder at the highest $\Fr$, is
consistent with a free-surface contribution. However, the data cannot
separate it from a Reynolds number effect.
\todo{any free-surface observations or photographs?}

\section{Conclusions}
\label{sec:conclusions}

Drag and shedding frequency were measured on three surface-piercing
circular cylinders towed at $\Rey = \ReMin \times 10^3$--$\ReMax \times
10^3$. After rejecting one run with load cell drift:
\begin{enumerate}
\item The mean drag coefficient is $C_D = \CdMean \pm \CdStd$, with no
significant dependence on diameter, even though aspect ratio and blockage
each change by a factor of two between cylinders.
\item The run-to-run scatter (2--3\%) dominates the measurement
precision. It is roughly ten times the within-run random error.
\item The Strouhal number is $\St = \StMean \pm \StStd$, in agreement with
two-dimensional data.
\item Evaluating fluid properties at the actual water temperature changes
$\Rey$ by about \ReBiasPct\% compared with assuming 20~$^\circ$C.
\end{enumerate}
\todo{Add conclusions tied to the motivation in Sec.~\ref{sec:intro}, and
the planned next steps (repeat runs, blockage, free-surface visualization).}

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

The flow past a circular cylinder is the canonical bluff-body problem, and
its mean drag coefficient in the subcritical regime ($10^3 \lesssim \Rey
\lesssim 2 \times 10^5$) is well established, at roughly
$C_D \approx 1.0$--$1.2$ for a nominally two-dimensional cylinder
\citep{Wieselsberger1921, Roshko1961, Zdravkovich1997}. Over the same range
the wake sheds vortices at a nearly constant Strouhal number
$\St \approx 0.2$ \citep{Williamson1996, Norberg2003}.

Towing-tank measurements depart from this ideal in several ways. The
cylinder pierces the free surface, so the free surface can deform and add
wave-making drag as the Froude number increases
\citep{ChaplinTeigen2003}. The submerged end is free, and the finite aspect
ratio changes the wake and lowers the sectional drag near the tip
\citep{FoxWest1993}. The model also occupies a finite fraction of the tank
cross-section, which accelerates the flow around it and raises the apparent
drag \citep{Maskell1963, WestApelt1982}.

\todo{State the motivation: e.g., commissioning/validating the facility,
providing a benchmark dataset, or a teaching laboratory. The framing decides
which of the discussion points below to emphasize.}
Here we report drag and shedding-frequency measurements on three cylinder
diameters at a fixed immersed length. Varying the diameter changes the
Reynolds number, Froude number, aspect ratio and blockage together, and we
use this to bound how large each effect can be.

surface and was immersed to a depth of $L = \SubLength$~m, leaving a gap of

\section{Data reduction}
\label{sec:reduction}

Figure~\ref{fig:timeseries} shows a typical force record. For each run the
load cell voltage averaged over the first second, with the carriage at rest,
is taken as the zero and subtracted. The mean drag $F_D$ is the average over
$3 \le t < 8$~s, where the carriage is moving at constant speed and the
start-up transient has passed. The drag coefficient, Reynolds number and
diameter Froude number are
\begin{equation}
C_D = \frac{F_D}{\tfrac{1}{2}\rho U^2 D L}, \qquad
\Rey = \frac{U D}{\nu}, \qquad
\Fr = \frac{U}{\sqrt{g D}},
\end{equation}
where $U$ is the carriage speed. The density $\rho$ and kinematic viscosity
$\nu$ are evaluated at each run's water temperature using the formulations
of \citet{Tanaka2001} and \citet{Kestin1978}. With $\nu$ fixed at its
20~$^\circ$C value instead, $\Rey$ would be overestimated by
\ReBiasPct\% on average, because the water was 2.4--6.3~$^\circ$C colder.

shedding frequency.}
\label{fig:timeseries}
\end{figure}

The shedding frequency $f_s$ is obtained from the force spectrum over the
same window. The in-line (drag) force fluctuates at $2 f_s$, so the
Strouhal number is $\St = f_{\mathrm{peak}} D / (2U)$, where
$f_{\mathrm{peak}}$ is the dominant spectral peak. A 5~s window gives a
frequency resolution of 0.2~Hz. This corresponds to an uncertainty in
$\St$ of up to about $\pm 0.01$ at the lowest speeds, and less at higher
speeds.

\paragraph{Run screening.}
The force after the carriage has stopped ($11 \le t < 12$~s) is compared
with the zero measured before the run. For \NGood{} of the \NRuns{} runs
the two agree within \MaxDriftGood~mN. In run~\ExcludedRun{}
(50.8~mm, 0.8~m/s) the reading drifts steadily through the run and ends

log. Its apparent drag coefficient of \ExcludedCd{} is an outlier, and runs

Three components of the uncertainty in $C_D$ can be estimated from the

\begin{itemize}
\item \emph{Random error of the mean within a run.} Block averaging over
five 1~s blocks gives a standard error of at most \CdSemMaxPct\% of $C_D$.
\item \emph{Calibration.} The standard error of the fitted sensitivity is
at most \SensErrPct\%.
\item \emph{Run-to-run repeatability.} The standard deviation of $C_D$
about the mean for each cylinder is 2--3\% (Table~\ref{tab:cylinders}).
\end{itemize}
The run-to-run scatter is about ten times larger than the within-run
random error. It must therefore come from run-to-run differences in the
conditions, such as residual tank motion from previous runs (noted in the
log for run~4) or small variations in carriage speed. We take it as the
measure of precision. \todo{add bias contributions from carriage speed

\label{sec:results}

\subsection{Drag coefficient}

Figure~\ref{fig:cd} shows the drag coefficients of all runs against
Reynolds and Froude numbers. Averaged over all \NGood{} accepted runs,
$C_D = \CdMean \pm \CdStd$. The means for the three cylinders
(\CdOne, \CdOneHalf{} and \CdTwo) differ by much less than the
run-to-run scatter. The aspect ratio varies by a factor of two and the
blockage ratio by a factor of two between cylinders, so within the
precision of these data, $C_D$ does not depend on diameter.

There is a weak upward trend of $C_D$ with speed. Over all accepted runs
the correlation coefficient of $C_D$ with $\ln \Rey$ is \CdReCorr, and with
$\Fr$ it is \CdFrCorr. The trend is clearest for the 25.4~mm cylinder,
which reaches the highest Froude numbers. For a single cylinder $\Rey$ and
$\Fr$ are both proportional to $U$, so the two cannot be separated within
one cylinder. Between cylinders, the 50.8~mm cylinder covers the largest
range of $\Rey$ at the smallest $\Fr$ and shows no clear trend.
\todo{decide whether the data support attributing the trend to $\Fr$; a

\subsection{Strouhal number}

The force spectrum has a single dominant peak in every run, and the
corresponding Strouhal numbers are plotted in Fig.~\ref{fig:st}. Across
all cylinders and speeds $\St = \StMean \pm \StStd$, independent of
$\Rey$, $\Fr$ and diameter within the frequency resolution. This value
agrees with the established subcritical value of $\St \approx 0.2$
\citep{Williamson1996, Norberg2003}. It also indicates that the dominant
force fluctuation is vortex shedding rather than a structural or carriage
resonance.

\label{fig:st}
\end{figure}

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Comparison with two-dimensional data.}
The measured $C_D = \CdMean$ is at the upper end of the
$C_D \approx 1.0$--$1.2$ range reported for nominally two-dimensional
cylinders at these Reynolds numbers \citep{Wieselsberger1921,
Zdravkovich1997}. Three effects specific to this setup push in different
directions.

\paragraph{Blockage.}
The frontal area of the immersed cylinder, $DL$, occupies
$B = \BlockageOne$--$\BlockageTwo$\% of the tank cross-section. As an
indication of the size of the effect, Maskell's correction
\citep{Maskell1963},
\begin{equation}
C_{D,c} = \frac{C_D}{1 + \varepsilon\, C_D\, B},
\label{eq:maskell}
\end{equation}
with $\varepsilon = \MaskellEps$, lowers the mean to
$C_{D,c} = \CdMaskellMean$. The corrected values for the three cylinders
(Table~\ref{tab:cylinders}) are more spread out than the uncorrected ones,
and the order is reversed, so that $C_{D,c}$ decreases with diameter.
Equation~\eqref{eq:maskell} was derived for closed wind tunnels. Its use
for a surface-piercing cylinder with a free end, in a tank with a free
surface, is uncertain. Some of the blocked fluid can escape through the
gap under the cylinder and by raising the free surface, so the
correction here is probably an upper bound. \todo{decide on a blockage
treatment, e.g.\ following \citet{WestApelt1982}, who found blockage
effects on circular cylinders to be small below $B \approx 6\%$; or report
uncorrected values only.}

\paragraph{Free end and aspect ratio.}
For cantilevered cylinders with a free end, the mean drag decreases as the
aspect ratio is reduced, because flow over the tip weakens the near-wake
suction \citep{FoxWest1993}. Here $L/D$ ranges from \AROne{} to \ARTwo{}.
A free-end effect alone would give the 50.8~mm cylinder the lowest $C_D$.
Instead the uncorrected means are flat in $D$, which is consistent with
the free-end and blockage effects partly cancelling.

\paragraph{Free surface.}
The diameter Froude number reaches \FrMax. At these Froude numbers the
free surface around a surface-piercing cylinder deforms strongly, with a
bow wave ahead and a depression behind, and the sectional drag near the
surface changes \citep{ChaplinTeigen2003}. The weak rise of $C_D$ with
speed, clearest for the smallest cylinder at the highest $\Fr$, is
consistent with a free-surface contribution. However, the data cannot
separate it from a Reynolds number effect.
\todo{any free-surface observations or photographs?}

\section{Conclusions}
\label{sec:conclusions}

Drag and shedding frequency were measured on three surface-piercing
circular cylinders towed at $\Rey = \ReMin \times 10^3$--$\ReMax \times
10^3$. After rejecting one run with load cell drift:
\begin{enumerate}
\item The mean drag coefficient is $C_D = \CdMean \pm \CdStd$, with no
significant dependence on diameter, even though aspect ratio and blockage
each change by a factor of two between cylinders.
\item The run-to-run scatter (2--3\%) dominates the measurement
precision. It is roughly ten times the within-run random error.
\item The Strouhal number is $\St = \StMean \pm \StStd$, in agreement with
two-dimensional data.
\item Evaluating fluid properties at the actual water temperature changes
$\Rey$ by about \ReBiasPct\% compared with assuming 20~$^\circ$C.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

The flow past a circular cylinder is the canonical bluff-body problem, and
its mean drag coefficient in the subcritical regime ($10^3 \lesssim \Rey
\lesssim 2 \times 10^5$) is well established, at roughly
$C_D \approx 1.0$--$1.2$ for a nominally two-dimensional cylinder
\citep{Wieselsberger1921, Roshko1961, Zdravkovich1997}. Over the same range
the wake sheds vortices at a nearly constant Strouhal number
$\St \approx 0.2$ \citep{Williamson1996, Norberg2003}.

Towing-tank measurements depart from this ideal in several ways. The
cylinder pierces the free surface, so the free surface can deform and add
wave-making drag as the Froude number increases
\citep{ChaplinTeigen2003}. The submerged end is free, and the finite aspect
ratio changes the wake and lowers the sectional drag near the tip
\citep{FoxWest1993}. The model also occupies a finite fraction of the tank
cross-section, which accelerates the flow around it and raises the apparent
drag \citep{Maskell1963, WestApelt1982}.

\section{Data reduction}
\label{sec:reduction}

Figure~\ref{fig:timeseries} shows a typical force record. For each run the
load cell voltage averaged over the first second, with the carriage at rest,
is taken as the zero and subtracted. The mean drag $F_D$ is the average over
$3 \le t < 8$~s, where the carriage is moving at constant speed and the
start-up transient has passed. The drag coefficient, Reynolds number and
diameter Froude number are
\begin{equation}
C_D = \frac{F_D}{\tfrac{1}{2}\rho U^2 D L}, \qquad
\Rey = \frac{U D}{\nu}, \qquad
\Fr = \frac{U}{\sqrt{g D}},
\end{equation}
where $U$ is the carriage speed. The density $\rho$ and kinematic viscosity
$\nu$ are evaluated at each run's water temperature using the formulations
of \citet{Tanaka2001} and \citet{Kestin1978}. With $\nu$ fixed at its
20~$^\circ$C value instead, $\Rey$ would be overestimated by
\ReBiasPct\% on average, because the water was 2.4--6.3~$^\circ$C colder.

\label{fig:timeseries}

The shedding frequency $f_s$ is obtained from the force spectrum over the
same window. The in-line (drag) force fluctuates at $2 f_s$, so the
Strouhal number is $\St = f_{\mathrm{peak}} D / (2U)$, where
$f_{\mathrm{peak}}$ is the dominant spectral peak. A 5~s window gives a
frequency resolution of 0.2~Hz. This corresponds to an uncertainty in
$\St$ of up to about $\pm 0.01$ at the lowest speeds, and less at higher
speeds.

\section{Results}
\label{sec:results}

\subsection{Drag coefficient}

Figure~\ref{fig:cd} shows the drag coefficients of all runs against
Reynolds and Froude numbers. Averaged over all \NGood{} accepted runs,
$C_D = \CdMean \pm \CdStd$. The means for the three cylinders
(\CdOne, \CdOneHalf{} and \CdTwo) differ by much less than the
run-to-run scatter. The aspect ratio varies by a factor of two and the
blockage ratio by a factor of two between cylinders, so within the
precision of these data, $C_D$ does not depend on diameter.

There is a weak upward trend of $C_D$ with speed. Over all accepted runs
the correlation coefficient of $C_D$ with $\ln \Rey$ is \CdReCorr, and with
$\Fr$ it is \CdFrCorr. The trend is clearest for the 25.4~mm cylinder,
which reaches the highest Froude numbers. For a single cylinder $\Rey$ and
$\Fr$ are both proportional to $U$, so the two cannot be separated within
one cylinder. Between cylinders, the 50.8~mm cylinder covers the largest
range of $\Rey$ at the smallest $\Fr$ and shows no clear trend.

The force spectrum has a single dominant peak in every run, and the

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Comparison with two-dimensional data.}
The measured $C_D = \CdMean$ is at the upper end of the
$C_D \approx 1.0$--$1.2$ range reported for nominally two-dimensional
cylinders at these Reynolds numbers \citep{Wieselsberger1921,
Zdravkovich1997}. Three effects specific to this setup push in different
directions.

\paragraph{Blockage.}
The frontal area of the immersed cylinder, $DL$, occupies
$B = \BlockageOne$--$\BlockageTwo$\% of the tank cross-section. As an
indication of the size of the effect, Maskell's correction
\citep{Maskell1963},
\begin{equation}
C_{D,c} = \frac{C_D}{1 + \varepsilon\, C_D\, B},
\label{eq:maskell}
\end{equation}
with $\varepsilon = \MaskellEps$, lowers the mean to
$C_{D,c} = \CdMaskellMean$. The corrected values for the three cylinders
(Table~\ref{tab:cylinders}) are more spread out than the uncorrected ones,
and the order is reversed, so that $C_{D,c}$ decreases with diameter.
Equation~\eqref{eq:maskell} was derived for closed wind tunnels. Its use
for a surface-piercing cylinder with a free end, in a tank with a free
surface, is uncertain. Some of the blocked fluid can escape through the
gap under the cylinder and by raising the free surface, so the
correction here is probably an upper bound. \todo{decide on a blockage
treatment, e.g.\ following \citet{WestApelt1982}, who found blockage
effects on circular cylinders to be small below $B \approx 6\%$; or report
uncorrected values only.}

\paragraph{Free end and aspect ratio.}
For cantilevered cylinders with a free end, the mean drag decreases as the
aspect ratio is reduced, because flow over the tip weakens the near-wake
suction \citep{FoxWest1993}. Here $L/D$ ranges from \AROne{} to \ARTwo{}.
A free-end effect alone would give the 50.8~mm cylinder the lowest $C_D$.
Instead the uncorrected means are flat in $D$, which is consistent with
the free-end and blockage effects partly cancelling.

\paragraph{Free surface.}
The diameter Froude number reaches \FrMax. At these Froude numbers the
free surface around a surface-piercing cylinder deforms strongly, with a
bow wave ahead and a depression behind, and the sectional drag near the
surface changes \citep{ChaplinTeigen2003}. The weak rise of $C_D$ with
speed, clearest for the smallest cylinder at the highest $\Fr$, is
consistent with a free-surface contribution. However, the data cannot
separate it from a Reynolds number effect.
\todo{any free-surface observations or photographs?}

\section{Conclusions}
\label{sec:conclusions}

Drag and shedding frequency were measured on three surface-piercing
circular cylinders towed at $\Rey = \ReMin \times 10^3$--$\ReMax \times
10^3$. After rejecting one run with load cell drift:
\begin{enumerate}
\item The mean drag coefficient is $C_D = \CdMean \pm \CdStd$, with no
significant dependence on diameter, even though aspect ratio and blockage
each change by a factor of two between cylinders.
\item The run-to-run scatter (2--3\%) dominates the measurement
precision. It is roughly ten times the within-run random error.
\item The Strouhal number is $\St = \StMean \pm \StStd$, in agreement with
two-dimensional data.
\item Evaluating fluid properties at the actual water temperature changes
$\Rey$ by about \ReBiasPct\% compared with assuming 20~$^\circ$C.
\end{enumerate}

"""Reduce raw tow tank load cell time series to mean drag force per run.

Handles both DAQ file formats (comma-separated with a commented header for
the 2025 batches, semicolon-separated for the 2026 batch) and fits the load
cell sensitivity from the calibration file in effect on the run date.

Outputs results/forces.csv and results/calibration.json.
"""

import glob
import json
import os

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

RAW_DIR = "data/raw"
CAL_DIR = "data/calibration"
OUT_DIR = "results"

G = 9.81
FS = 200.0  # Hz, sample rate for both DAQ versions
TARE_WINDOW = (0.0, 1.0)  # s, carriage at rest before the run
STEADY_WINDOW = (3.0, 8.0)  # s, constant carriage speed
POST_WINDOW = (11.0, 12.0)  # s, carriage at rest after the run
N_BLOCKS = 5  # blocks for standard error of the steady-state mean

# Calibration in effect for each batch (load cell remounted 2026-03-10)
CALIBRATIONS = {
    "2025-10-14": "loadcell_2025-09.csv",
    "2025-11-03": "loadcell_2025-09.csv",
    "2026-03-12": "loadcell_2026-03.csv",
}


def fit_calibration(fname):
    cal = pd.read_csv(os.path.join(CAL_DIR, fname))
    force = cal.mass_g / 1000 * G
    (slope, intercept), cov = np.polyfit(force, cal.voltage_V, 1, cov=True)
    resid = cal.voltage_V - (slope * force + intercept)
    return {
        "file": fname,
        "sensitivity_V_per_N": float(slope),
        "sensitivity_std_err": float(np.sqrt(cov[0, 0])),
        "offset_V": float(intercept),
        "max_resid_N": float(np.abs(resid).max() / slope),
        "max_load_N": float(force.max()),
        "n_points": len(cal),
    }


def read_run(fname):
    """Return (time_s, voltage_V) for either DAQ file format."""
    with open(fname) as f:
        first = f.readline()
    if ";" in first:
        d = pd.read_csv(fname, sep=";")
        return d.t.values, d.V.values
    d = pd.read_csv(fname, comment="#")
    return d.time_s.values, d.loadcell_V.values


def in_window(t, window):
    return (t >= window[0]) & (t < window[1])


def dominant_frequency(x):
    n = np.arange(len(x))
    x = x - np.polyval(np.polyfit(n, x, 1), n)
    power = np.abs(np.fft.rfft(x * np.hanning(len(x)))) ** 2
    freqs = np.fft.rfftfreq(len(x), 1 / FS)
    return freqs[np.argmax(power[1:]) + 1]


cals = {name: fit_calibration(name) for name in sorted(set(CALIBRATIONS.values()))}
for c in cals.values():
    print(f"{c['file']}: sensitivity = {c['sensitivity_V_per_N']:.5f} V/N")

rows = []
for batch, cal_file in CALIBRATIONS.items():
    sens = cals[cal_file]["sensitivity_V_per_N"]
    for fname in sorted(glob.glob(os.path.join(RAW_DIR, batch, "run_*.csv"))):
        t, v = read_run(fname)
        tare = v[in_window(t, TARE_WINDOW)].mean()
        post = v[in_window(t, POST_WINDOW)].mean()
        force = (v - tare) / sens
        steady = force[in_window(t, STEADY_WINDOW)]
        block_means = np.array([b.mean() for b in np.array_split(steady, N_BLOCKS)])
        rows.append({
            "run": int(os.path.basename(fname)[4:7]),
            "batch": batch,
            "calibration": cal_file,
            "sensitivity_V_per_N": sens,
            "F_mean_N": steady.mean(),
            "F_std_N": steady.std(),
            "F_sem_N": block_means.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(N_BLOCKS),
            "zero_drift_N": (post - tare) / sens,
            "f_peak_Hz": dominant_frequency(steady),
        })

os.makedirs(OUT_DIR, exist_ok=True)
out = pd.DataFrame(rows).sort_values("run")
out.to_csv(os.path.join(OUT_DIR, "forces.csv"), index=False)
with open(os.path.join(OUT_DIR, "calibration.json"), "w") as f:
    json.dump(cals, f, indent=2)
print(f"Processed {len(out)} runs")

"""Reduce raw tow tank load cell time series to mean drag force per run.

Handles both DAQ file formats (comma-separated with a commented header for
the 2025 batches, semicolon-separated for the 2026 batch) and fits the load
cell sensitivity from the calibration file in effect on the run date.

Outputs results/forces.csv and results/calibration.json.
"""

import glob
import json
import os

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

RAW_DIR = "data/raw"
CAL_DIR = "data/calibration"
OUT_DIR = "results"

G = 9.81
FS = 200.0  # Hz, sample rate for both DAQ versions
TARE_WINDOW = (0.0, 1.0)  # s, carriage at rest before the run
STEADY_WINDOW = (3.0, 8.0)  # s, constant carriage speed
POST_WINDOW = (11.0, 12.0)  # s, carriage at rest after the run
N_BLOCKS = 5  # blocks for standard error of the steady-state mean

# Calibration in effect for each batch (load cell remounted 2026-03-10)
CALIBRATIONS = {
    "2025-10-14": "loadcell_2025-09.csv",
    "2025-11-03": "loadcell_2025-09.csv",
    "2026-03-12": "loadcell_2026-03.csv",
}


def fit_calibration(fname):
    cal = pd.read_csv(os.path.join(CAL_DIR, fname))
    force = cal.mass_g / 1000 * G
    (slope, intercept), cov = np.polyfit(force, cal.voltage_V, 1, cov=True)
    resid = cal.voltage_V - (slope * force + intercept)
    return {
        "file": fname,
        "sensitivity_V_per_N": float(slope),
        "sensitivity_std_err": float(np.sqrt(cov[0, 0])),
        "offset_V": float(intercept),
        "max_resid_N": float(np.abs(resid).max() / slope),
        "max_load_N": float(force.max()),
        "n_points": len(cal),
    }


def read_run(fname):
    """Return (time_s, voltage_V) for either DAQ file format."""
    with open(fname) as f:
        first = f.readline()
    if ";" in first:
        d = pd.read_csv(fname, sep=";")
        return d.t.values, d.V.values
    d = pd.read_csv(fname, comment="#")
    return d.time_s.values, d.loadcell_V.values


def in_window(t, window):
    return (t >= window[0]) & (t < window[1])


def dominant_frequency(x):
    n = np.arange(len(x))
    x = x - np.polyval(np.polyfit(n, x, 1), n)
    power = np.abs(np.fft.rfft(x * np.hanning(len(x)))) ** 2
    freqs = np.fft.rfftfreq(len(x), 1 / FS)
    return freqs[np.argmax(power[1:]) + 1]


cals = {name: fit_calibration(name) for name in sorted(set(CALIBRATIONS.values()))}
for c in cals.values():
    print(f"{c['file']}: sensitivity = {c['sensitivity_V_per_N']:.5f} V/N")

rows = []
for batch, cal_file in CALIBRATIONS.items():
    sens = cals[cal_file]["sensitivity_V_per_N"]
    for fname in sorted(glob.glob(os.path.join(RAW_DIR, batch, "run_*.csv"))):
        t, v = read_run(fname)
        tare = v[in_window(t, TARE_WINDOW)].mean()
        post = v[in_window(t, POST_WINDOW)].mean()
        force = (v - tare) / sens
        steady = force[in_window(t, STEADY_WINDOW)]
        block_means = np.array([b.mean() for b in np.array_split(steady, N_BLOCKS)])
        rows.append({
            "run": int(os.path.basename(fname)[4:7]),
            "batch": batch,
            "calibration": cal_file,
            "sensitivity_V_per_N": sens,
            "F_mean_N": steady.mean(),
            "F_std_N": steady.std(),
            "F_sem_N": block_means.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(N_BLOCKS),
            "zero_drift_N": (post - tare) / sens,
            "f_peak_Hz": dominant_frequency(steady),
        })

os.makedirs(OUT_DIR, exist_ok=True)
out = pd.DataFrame(rows).sort_values("run")
out.to_csv(os.path.join(OUT_DIR, "forces.csv"), index=False)
with open(os.path.join(OUT_DIR, "calibration.json"), "w") as f:
    json.dump(cals, f, indent=2)
print(f"Processed {len(out)} runs")

I checked the draft against all three comments. The current version already deals with each of them, so I didn't change anything. The pipeline reports up to date (`calkit status`: "Pipeline is up to date"), so the generated numbers, tables and figures match the code and data.

**Reviewer 1.1 (viscosity at 20 °C):** Already done. `scripts/analyze.py` works out ρ and ν for each run from that run's logged water temperature (13.7–17.6 °C), using the Kestin et al. (1978) and Tanaka et al. (2001) formulas. I hand-checked the viscosity formula and one Reynolds number: run 1 comes out at 4.7×10³. The paper says this in the Data reduction section and adds that a fixed 20 °C value would have overstated Re by about 12% on average. It also lists each run's temperature in Table 1 and the appendix table.

**Reviewer 1.2 (run 17):** Already done. Run 17 is **excluded**, not corrected, and the paper says so under "Run screening." Its zero drifted by 4.2 N during the run, against at most 3.5 mN for every other run, and its apparent C_D of 1.35 is an outlier. The abstract and conclusions mention the exclusion, the C_D figure shows it as an open symbol, and the appendix table marks it with †. The other 2 in. runs give C_D = 1.157 ± 0.034.

**Reviewer 2.1 (Re range in abstract):** Already done. The abstract gives Re_D = 4.7×10³–49.8×10³, along with the Froude number range.

The reviewers were probably reading an older version, most likely one built from the original notebook. That workflow used ν at 20 °C and kept run 17 in the averages; `notes.md` records 1.18 for the 2 in. cylinder from it. The first commit of `paper.tex` already contains all three fixes, so it's worth checking which PDF went to the journal.

For the response letter, you can answer each comment with "already addressed in the revised manuscript" and point to the sections above. I can draft that letter if you'd like. One optional extra for 1.2: the drift in run 17 is described as steady, so a linear drift correction might be possible, but excluding the run is simpler to defend.
